newsitem.title: UK: UK builders reject Lang's Social Chapter doom.
newsitem.headline: UK builders reject Lang's Social Chapter doom.

text.p: British trade and industry minister Ian Lang said on Tuesday that construction jobs and prosperity would be at risk if the European Social Chapter were adopted in the country.
But industry leaders rejected the warning as "an electioneering red herring".
Lang attacked the Social Chapter, from which Britain has opted out, in a speech to the Chartered Institute of Building.
"If we signed up to the Social Chapter we would open ourselves to a pipeline bulging with future burdens on business," he told the Institute's annual dinner.
British building companies could find themselves facing the kind of job losses seen in Germany.
"Last month alone half a million Germans lost their jobs. And it is no coincidence that the construction industry is among the worst hit by the mounting uncompetitiveness there," he said.
Building bosses contradicted Lang's pessimistic view.
Graham Watts, chief executive of the Construction Industry Council, said: "This is nothing more than an electioneering red-herring."
"The impact of the Social Chapter has been hyped up to satisfy Conservative Party's europhobia," he added.

An election is due by May 22, with the opposition Labour Party, currently leading in opinion polls, committed to entering the EU Social Chapter. Watts said the British construction industry was far from prosperous and had only just seen tentative signs of recovery after more than five years of recession.
"He talks of half a million jobs lost in Germany. That is exactly the amount the British construction industry has lost in the last five years," Watts said.
Paul Shepherd, chairman of the Building Employers Confederation (BEC), announced earlier on Tuesday that total output in 1996 was up just 0.4 percent in 1996, after years of decline.
He had also told reporters that EU labour legislation was unlikely to have an effect on the industry.
This was later echoed by a BEC spokesman. "This is a manageable issue. We don't think it would have much impact," he told Reuters.
Lang criticised the impact of the 48 hour working week limit under EU law.

"The Working Time Directive is also bad for employers, bad for employees and bad for industry. It would hit the construction industry particularly hard, replacing flexibility with rigidity and bureaucracy," he said.
But the BEC spokesman said that the issue had already been discussed with unions in an effort to work around the law and he did not envisage problems stemming from the EU legislation.
The industry had been far from booming in recent years. "We've only just emerged from recession," he said.

The building industry has lost 500,000 jobs in the last five years and seen construction prices falling in real terms since 1991. Profit margins have been razor thin, forcing many British firms to seek contracts overseas where the margins are better but the risks higher.
